text: Let's learn about adding two numbers. When we add, we put things together. If you have 3 apples and your friend gives you 2 more, you now have 5 apples. We write this as 3 + 2 = 5. You can count on your fingers to check. Start at 3 and count up two more: 4, 5. Adding is the same in any order, so 2 + 3 is also 5.

Today we will look at shapes. A triangle has three sides and three corners. A square has four sides that are all the same length. A rectangle also has four sides, but two are long and two are short. A circle has no corners at all. Look around your room. Can you find a shape like a square? A window or a book might be one.

In this lesson, we will learn how to tell time. A clock has a short hand and a long hand. The short hand shows the hour. The long hand shows the minutes. When the long hand points to 12, it is the start of a new hour. If the short hand is on 3 and the long hand is on 12, it is three o'clock.

Let's think about money. A penny is worth one cent. A nickel is worth five cents. A dime is worth ten cents, and a quarter is worth twenty-five cents. If you have two dimes and one nickel, you have twenty-five cents. That is the same as one quarter. Counting coins is a good way to practice adding.

Plants and animals are living things. Living things grow, need food and water, and make more of their own kind. A rock is not living. It does not eat or grow. A dog is living because it eats, drinks and grows from a puppy into a big dog. Can you name three living things you saw today?

Let's practice comparing numbers. We use the sign > to say a number is greater. We use < to say a number is less. For example, 7 > 4 because seven is more than four. And 2 < 9 because two is less than nine. A trick is to think of the sign as a hungry mouth that always eats the bigger number.
